title: AI brute-forces a Putnam problem with thousands of lines of Lean code — this is not a victory for intelligence
dek: The Putnam had produced only five perfect scores in 98 years; AI just got the sixth, but it didn't take the human route — it enumerated its way through thousands of lines of Lean. Automated theorem proving existed long before AI.
why: Hong Lechong rarely talks about the real demerits of deep tech startups, the group-game mechanics of fundraising, and why translating math into Lean is harder than the proof itself.
who: For founders doing deep tech or AI for Science, investors watching early-stage fundraising games, and engineers who want the frontier of formal mathematics meeting AI.
skip: If constitutional interpretation and founder typologies don't interest you, skip the two segments at 1:04:26 and 18:05.

points.h: AI got a perfect score, but it didn't take the human route
points.body: Axiom's Action Prover scored a perfect score on the Putnam, the university-level math competition. The competition began in 1927, and in the past 98 years only five humans have ever scored perfect — this is the sixth, and it went to AI. What's interesting is the comparison of solutions: Evan Chen (coach of the US IMO team) drew a single diagram and solved one of the problems, but the AI never found that solution. Instead it used thousands of lines of Lean code, grinding it out step by step through something like enumeration and case analysis. Hong Lechong calls this ‘brute force that produces miracles’ — even for a problem that clearly admits a creative solution, the machine will take the path it's good at and arrive at a completely different one.

points.h: Automated theorem proving is not a victory for AI
points.body: Hong Lechong corrects a common misconception: the field of automated theorem proving (ATP) existed before deep neural networks, before AI — it was a group of computer scientists hoping to use rule-based systems to help humans solve math problems. ITP is interactive theorem proving, historically done by human mathematicians working with computer systems. What's happening now is just replacing the human in ITP with AI. So this old discipline is essentially the intersection of ATP and AI, and it can't be counted as a victory for AI.

points.h: The ratio of bounded attention to free attention
points.body: Hong Lechong's advisor proposed a pair of concepts: bounded attention is attention that's framed, like the emails and deadlines you have to process every morning; free attention is free attention, and many successful entrepreneurs are extremely disciplined executors, compounding execution day after day. But what separates an average founder from one who makes strategic decisions is precisely free attention. She stresses this isn't linear — you can spend time on free attention and think of nothing, but later, when forced into a task, there's a callback, returning to the foundation free attention laid down for the brain. The ratio varies from person to person; she doesn't know her own.

points.h: Jumping from constitutional interpretation to AI doing math
points.body: While studying constitutional interpretation in law school, Hong Lechong encountered three interpretive approaches — originalism, textualism, living constitutionalism — and she considers herself a textualist. Someone suggested feeding language models data like the founding documents to understand word meanings, and from there she thought: if AI can already see what the Constitution means, why can't AI do math? Because math doesn't need English, it needs a more structural presentation, and formal language turns math into code. One of her best friends, Kenny Law, has been doing Lean formal proofs since 2020, is one of the first five to seven builders of Mathlib, and is a student of Kevin Buzzard.

points.h: A mathematician background may be a demerit for a scaling team
points.body: Axiom set a rule early on: don't hire mathematicians until the 15th person, because the seed round was an under raise relative to what they wanted to do, and headcount was constrained. More crucially, some classmates with math backgrounds were hesitant about scaling, or even disliked the philosophy, feeling math is a craft, like a Japanese master making sushi. Some accepted an offer and then didn't come, saying they didn't want to work on an Internet Scale Dataset. So now hiring mathematicians requires very open-minded thinking, and they want them to do adversarial benchmark creation, working against the system, to feel where the system is weak. After Ken Ono joined, he became the number one figure in the benchmark-level assembly.

points.h: Fundraising is a group game; nobody wants to reject first
points.body: Hong Lechong describes investors' real behavior during fundraising: they don't reject you directly, they stall you — because they're afraid that after rejecting you won't talk to them again, so they wait until you have someone else's offer and then follow. She calls this mechanism groupthink. So what the founder really has to solve isn't ‘convincing everyone’, but finding a lead investor willing to say yes first; the rest will oversubscribe. In her seed round she got three lead offers at once, and the price went from one multiple to two to three, one step up per month.

points.h: There's too little Lean data; you have to build the verification tools yourself
points.body: Lean is a formal language, and the total token volume in the public domain is very small, nowhere near comparable to Python. It's simultaneously a programming language, a compiler and a runtime, and it's very finicky — objects must satisfy all sorts of constraints. She also points out the cheating risk: if you assume the axiom n plus n equals n, you can ‘prove’ 2 plus 2 equals 2. The comparator the community used before was a hundred times slower than their self-developed verify proof, so they built twelve or thirteen auxiliary tools. AlphaProof uses Monte Carlo tree search, which they consider too expensive — they don't have the money, so they had to find another way.

points.h: Translating math into Lean is harder than proving it
points.body: She believes auto formalization is severely underestimated: turning paired theorems and proofs from arXiv papers into Lean code requires first extracting a blueprint, and a 20-page article may split into 200 to 500 pages. Terence Tao, Kevin Buzzard and Alex Kontorovich once wrote blueprints by hand, then distributed them to undergraduates around the world, each taking a small piece. She points out this isn't translation — English and French have similar levels of abstraction, whereas Lean is more like Python, and AI has seen very little Lean data. The reverse direction, auto-informalization, is easier, but you need cycle consistency to repeatedly turn it back and verify correctness.

quotes.text: In 2024, AlphaProof came out of nowhere and got 28 points, a silver medal one point short of gold. For me that was the moment IMO was solved.
It's just tiring. You're a parrot, saying the same thing over and over, getting the same question over and over.
Doing product when you're young is a plus; doing deep tech when you're young is a demerit.
People haven't realized one thing: we are not a model company, we are a deep tech company, a deep science and technology company. What we're doing is a bit like SpaceX.
Now is not the moment for the pure beauty of mathematics. Don't go precisely fiddling with these things. Now is a state of war.

But if you just take the mathematics that humans have already discovered and written down and convert it into this formalized form, you'll get less praise. But this technology is actually harder than the proof, at least as hard — I actually think it's harder.
